title: I built an add-on that can tell you if an appliance is on when it shouldn't be, or even about to fail!
text: If you have a multi-channel energy meter this (HACS) add-on analyzes appliance energy patterns, and creates sensors that can be used for notifications to tell you when an appliance is acting differently than it normally does. It can answer questions like the following: * Is this appliance running, idle, on standby, or not showing recent activity? * Is today's energy use unusually high for this circuit? * Is my refrigerator, washer, dryer, pump, HVAC, water heater, or EV charger behaving differently from its learned baseline? * Is a 240 V appliance balanced across both legs? * Are watts, amps, volts, VA, and power factor internally consistent? * Is a circuit approaching a configured breaker o

top.b: Wasn't sure how much detail you wanted. No, it does not use an LLM to do anything. The pattern matching is a rule-based time-series with robust baseline comparison using median, median absolute deviation, 10th percentile, 90th percentile, and a confidence value based on sample count. Deviation scoring compares the observed value against the baseline median using a spread based on MAD, a percentage of the median, and a minimum floor. It'll gather data for x (default 7) number

title: Home Assistant app that estimates appliance usage from one mains power sensor
text: Most appliance-level energy monitoring in Home Assistant means adding a smart plug, clamp meter, or submeter for every device. That gets expensive fast, and it is not always practical for hardwired or high-current appliances. I built a NILM (Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring) project that uses a single whole-home mains power sensor to estimate when individual appliances are running and their approximate power use. You train a model on your own Home Assistant history, so it can adapt to your appliances and electrical setup. It can then publish virtual entities for estimated appliance power, cumulative energy consumption, and on/off state. These can be used in dashboards, automations, notification

Thank you for the feedback. You can train it either with a ground-truth appliance power meter or by manually marking the appliance’s ON intervals. The website has short explanatory videos that walk through both approaches: [https://ha-nilm.bigwicho.com/](https://ha-nilm.bigwicho.com/)

Thank you. The 4 GB recommendation is an estimate for running both the NILM and Training Server apps on the same device. You may need less RAM when training with a shorter data interval, such as one to three days. If the Training Server runs on another machine, I estimate that the NILM app can run on the Home Assistant device with around 1 GB of RAM.

The main NILM app requires the Home Assistant OS app/add-on environment, including Supervisor/Ingress support, which Home Assistant Container does not provide. The training server can run as Docker, but the main NILM app is not yet supported as a standalone container. Container support may be added later. EDIT: this can work when the containers are run directly, and you manually provide the HA API URL, WebSocket URL, and a long-lived access token.

title: Estimate Appliance Energy Use From Whole Home Power, Now With Multiple Mains Support | HA-NILM 1.1.9
text: Hey everyone, For anyone discovering it for the first time, HA-NILM is a local Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring system for Home Assistant. It uses your whole-home power data and a short training process to estimate when individual appliances are running and how much energy they use. I’ve just released **HA NILM 1.1.9**, with support for multiple mains sensors. # What’s new **Multiple mains sensors** You can now configure multiple mains power sensors, making HA-NILM suitable for split phase, three phase, multiple meters, and independently monitored panel setups. Each appliance model can be assigned to the mains sensor that actually powers it, and inference is performed using that specific feed.

top.b: I have most things monitored in the house, except for the oven, kettle, coffee machines and air fryer. Would this be useful for tracking their usage?

Yes, absolutely. It has already been tested with kettles and ovens and works well with them. That said, it is still something worth testing on each setup because appliances can have very different power signatures depending on the model and how they operate.

title: Anomaly detection in power consumption + NILM
text: Hey, for a project I have data of total energy consumption over time as well as the data of individual sensors reading the consumption of IoTs. I want to use unsupervised anomaly detection on the total data and identify which sensor is most responsible. For anomaly detection, I tried simple methods like z-score; however, given that the data is not normally distributed, I went with isolation forest. Now, for assigning sensors to the anomalies, I tried to look at their rate of change around the timestep of the anomalies, but I am not confident in my results yet. Does anyone have any other suggestions on how to tackle this?

top.b: With isoforest you need to set an anomaly rate. How did you determine that number?
i first used 0.01 as a starting point which seemed to mark too many datapoints as anomalies and gradually lowered it. I have no labeled data so it is a bit hard to determine the ideal parameter.

Are the anomalies fundamentally time based? Or like range based? If time based try fft detection methods for anomalies. If range based you can try clustering algos, AE, or boosted trees. Don’t be afraid to diff sensor 1 / sensor 2, stuff like that. Another one to try if time based is matrix profiling; check out stumpy library. With clustering / AE you are looking for different groups or areas with high reconstruction error. You could try and select periods you THINK are good
thanks for the suggestions i will look into it! What do you recommend for finding the sensor that is causing the anomaly? Is looking at differences around an anomaly feasable?

title: Energy Disaggregation at the Home
text: I started collecting data about energy use in my home using a few smart plugs on particular appliances, but I wanted the whole picture. This led to buying an energy monitor that has a current transformer (CT) clamp on each leg of my split single phase supply coming into my breaker box. This allows me to see the aggregate usage for the whole house (or for each leg of the split phase). I have this data flowing into Home Assistant and InfluxDB. I’d like to be able to account for the energy use of different loads in the house, or in other words, to disaggregate the energy use data that I’m collecting. I have also seen this referred to as non-intrusive load monitoring. For anyone with experience

top.b: many of the lectric loads would be step loads, step on, step off, at an approximately the same amount, as in +2000W load, the kettle on, and -2000W kettle off. Refridgerators will tend off to have exponential decay, as in 120W load, decreasing to 77W, then step off to 5-6W etc.
Big motors or anything with a heating element are usually the biggest draws. If it's an old house, you could probably upgrade windows, insulation, washer, and swap any lights to led.

>I have this data flowing into Home Assistant and InfluxDB. I Oh my! Big data for a small house! :) You need to understand the behavior of your individual loads if you want to have a signal analysis if what I am reading is correct. As in, does your load modulate its power input? Does it change? In steps or continuously? When a 20W load jump appears, is it a light bulb? DOes it disappear into another 20W step down? Etc. Refridgerators act weird. etc.

The big loads would probably be the easiest to identify, especially if they have a clear on/off profile or very regular intervals. I expect it is much more difficult to identify the always-on loads or small loads with irregular usage patterns.
